Yes — **[writing-clearly-and-concisely](https://www.skills.sh/softaworks/agent-toolkit/writing-clearly-and-concisely)** is my pick for you.

I checked its actual instructions. It explicitly covers READMEs and teaches agents to:

- Cut needless words and use concrete, direct language.
- Remove marketing fluff like “groundbreaking,” “seamless,” and “robust.”
- Avoid typical AI vocabulary, excessive bullets, and emoji decorations. [Source](https://github.com/softaworks/agent-toolkit/blob/main/skills/writing-clearly-and-concisely/SKILL.md)

It has about **4.3K installs**, and its repository has **2.5K stars**. [Details](https://www.skills.sh/softaworks/agent-toolkit/writing-clearly-and-concisely)

Install it with:

```bash
npx skills add softaworks/agent-toolkit --skill writing-clearly-and-concisely
```

Then give the agent this instruction:

> Write the README like a developer explaining their project to another developer. Keep it short. Start with what it does, show installation and one working example. No hype, filler, or invented features.

Yes — I found **two worth using together**, and checked their actual instructions.

| Skill | Best for | Adoption |
|---|---|---|
| **[baoyu-format-markdown](https://www.skills.sh/jimliu/baoyu-skills/baoyu-format-markdown)** | Polishing Markdown: heading hierarchy, selective bold, tables, lists, code blocks, and visual breaks. Preserves your wording. | ~27.8K installs |
| **[crafting-effective-readmes](https://www.skills.sh/softaworks/agent-toolkit/crafting-effective-readmes)** | Organizing READMEs around the reader: clear description, quick start, useful examples, and sections suited to the project. | ~4.1K installs |

**My recommendation:** use `crafting-effective-readmes` for structure, plus the earlier `writing-clearly-and-concisely` for natural prose. Add `baoyu-format-markdown` for the formatting pass.

One caveat: Baoyu defaults to article-style frontmatter and title changes. For GitHub READMEs, explicitly tell it to **keep the H1 title and skip frontmatter**. [Instructions](https://github.com/JimLiu/baoyu-skills/blob/main/skills/baoyu-format-markdown/SKILL.md)

```bash
npx skills add softaworks/agent-toolkit --skill crafting-effective-readmes
npx skills add jimliu/baoyu-skills --skill baoyu-format-markdown
```

Use this prompt with them:

> Make this README clean, polished, and easy to scan. Use a clear heading hierarchy, short paragraphs, working code examples, and tables where they help. Keep bold selective. Preserve the H1 title; skip YAML frontmatter. Keep the writing direct and human.
run both of the commands for me + add the prompt in that skill directly
I’ll install both skills and add your README style preferences directly to their instructions.

I’m using the skill-installer and skill-creator guidance. I’ll install these for this repository and put the preferences in both `SKILL.md` files, including the README exception for Baoyu’s frontmatter defaults.

I’ll look for a language-agnostic skill that writes useful code comments and documents types, structs, classes, and public APIs.

The closest match I found is **[code-documentation](https://www.skills.sh/aj-geddes/useful-ai-prompts/code-documentation)** from `aj-geddes/useful-ai-prompts`.

I checked its instructions. It covers **classes, functions, type definitions, public APIs, and inline comments**, with guidance to explain intent, document errors and edge cases, and avoid obvious or excessive comments. It explicitly supports JSDoc, Python docstrings, and JavaDoc. [Source](https://github.com/aj-geddes/useful-ai-prompts/blob/main/skills/code-documentation/SKILL.md)

It has roughly **472 installs**; the repository has **355 stars**. It’s a promising match, though I couldn’t verify dedicated conventions for every language. [Skill details](https://www.skills.sh/aj-geddes/useful-ai-prompts/code-documentation), [repository](https://github.com/aj-geddes/useful-ai-prompts).

```bash
npx skills add aj-geddes/useful-ai-prompts --skill code-documentation
```

For your requirement, I’d add this directly to the skill:

> Apply across languages using each language’s native documentation conventions. Document public types, structs, classes, interfaces, object shapes, fields, constructors, and methods. Explain purpose, constraints, defaults, units, ownership, and errors where relevant. Keep comments concise and accurate. Explain non-obvious decisions; avoid repeating the code.
